steps.page: How I understand what you want
steps.intro: Judge here: is this what you want from review decks? I re-read all six of your chat messages and every answer on all eight decks. Mark each statement Holds or Fails; say what I got wrong.

steps.headline: A deck is where you steer. I decide only what no user could notice.
steps.changed: You decide layout, the path between screens and how parts affect each other. I decide code matters inside those decisions.
steps.notice: A deck never asks you about code, and never settles a design question without you.

steps.headline: One feature has one deck, on one link, that grows with the work.
steps.changed: It starts as "here is how I understand this", becomes the design, then the plan before building, then the results after. It is never replaced by a new deck each round.
steps.notice: You keep one link per feature. Opening it always shows where the feature stands now.

steps.headline: What you said earlier stays visible where it belongs, not behind a History button.
steps.changed: Each topic shows its own story in place: your words, what was built, what you said next. Settled topics shrink.
steps.notice: No History button, no "Details" fold, no New or Changed badges.

steps.headline: Every page is named for what you are deciding, never for my work.
steps.changed: Pages like "What the reviewers found" or "What slipped between rounds" describe my process. Pages should be the stages and topics of the feature.
steps.notice: You can tell from a page's name what it wants from you.

steps.headline: A card holds one kind of thing: facts, things you can change, or results.
steps.changed: Round 8 mixed plain rows, changeable rows and rows with a Passed or Unclear chip in one card.
steps.notice: Chips appear only on a results page, on every row of it. A question is always its own card with buttons.

steps.headline: A deck should look like part of YouCoded, with pictures large enough to read.
steps.changed: Only parts the app already has. You have asked for larger pictures in rounds 4, 5 and 8.
steps.notice: A picture opens at a size where its words can be read without zooming.

steps.headline: There is no contract or sign-off deck. The safety checks that came with it should not vanish silently.
steps.changed: Finished means: every request is a row before building, and you change nothing after. The old automatic checks need a home; the "safety net" page asks where.
steps.notice: Fewer decks to sign, without losing what the old checks caught.

steps.intro: Judge here: which shape should a growing deck take? Three drawings, each filled with this feature's real story. Press a picture to open it large. Pick one, and say what to borrow from another.

steps.path: Any deck, from its first round to the finished build
steps.headline: How should one deck grow with a feature?
steps.today: Each round is a new deck on a new link. Earlier rounds sit behind a History button, and a row's story hides in a "Details" fold.
steps.checked: Counted the nine decks of this work today and opened round 8.
steps.problem: You called it a sticky note. Nothing shows a feature moving from first idea to finished build, and you cannot tell what a page is for.
steps.proposal: Pick the shape. In all three there is one link, your earlier words stay visible, and each round's answers are still saved separately behind the scenes.

options.label: A. Stages across the top, topics stay in place
pros: The top shows where the feature is: Understanding, Design, Before build, After build.
Each topic carries its whole story where you answer it.
Settled topics shrink to one line, so the page shows what needs you.
cons: A topic argued over many rounds gets a long story above its answer.
I must keep topics matched across rounds; a renamed topic could lose its story.

options.label: B. One long document, newest round on top
pros: Simple to follow in time order.
An old round opens exactly as you left it.
cons: To follow one topic you open every round it appeared in.
Close to today's History, moved onto the page.

options.label: C. A list of topics at the left, one topic at a time
pros: The whole feature at a glance, with what needs you at the top.
One topic fills the page, so nothing else competes.
cons: More clicking: one topic per view.
On a phone the list becomes a menu you must open.

steps.intro: Judge here: are these the right three kinds of card, and how large should a picture open? Drawings, not built.

steps.headline: Should a card hold only one kind of row?
steps.today: One card can mix plain rows, rows you can change and rows with a Passed or Unclear chip. Extra notes sit in a "Details" fold.
steps.checked: Read your three round-8 comments and the picture you attached today.
steps.problem: You could not tell which rows were facts, which were questions and which were results, or what "Details" was for.
steps.proposal: Yes builds the three kinds in the picture: for your information, yours to change, results. "Details" goes; reuse notes sit behind a small (i). No keeps mixed cards.

steps.headline: How should a picture open?
steps.today: A picture opens in a full window, shrunk to fit, with comments at the right.
steps.checked: Your round-8 comment today: "90% of this popup page is unused dead space".
steps.problem: A tall screenshot shrinks until its words cannot be read, and most of the window is empty.
steps.proposal: Pick where comments sit. In both the picture opens at its true size and you scroll it. Both also need me to take pictures narrower and closer.

options.label: A. Comments in a strip at the right
pros: Comments stay in view while you scroll the picture.
Matches how the app shows a file with its comments.
cons: The picture gets three quarters of the width, not all of it.

options.label: B. Comments in a bar underneath
pros: The picture uses the whole width.
Works the same on a phone.
cons: On a tall picture the comments are below the fold.

steps.intro: Judge here: which checks from the old system come back, and where? The picture on the first question shows a feature from start to finish, with what is in place, what went away with the contract, and what is your call.

steps.headline: Which of the old automatic checks should come back?
steps.today: Dropping the contract also dropped four things: tracing each plan row to your answer, a fresh grader checking every request was built, reviewer findings shown as rows, and a check that refuses to close unfinished work.
steps.checked: Compared the old rule files with this branch's, line by line, today.
steps.problem: You approved dropping the contract deck, not these. In round 5 you said the grader would be "replaced or modified", not removed.
steps.proposal: Pick how much returns. None of it brings back a deck for you to sign; results appear as rows on the after-build page.

options.label: All four, as checks that are on unless you switch them off
pros: A missed request is caught by a fresh pair of eyes, not by you.
Unfinished work cannot be closed by mistake.
cons: Each build takes a little longer.
More rows on the after-build page.

options.label: Only the "was every request built?" check
pros: The one that catches the costliest mistake.
Least added waiting.
cons: Reviewer findings stay summed up in one status row.
Nothing stops unfinished work being closed.

options.label: Leave them out
pros: Fastest builds.
cons: You are the only check that a request was built.

steps.headline: Should a fresh-eyes tester try the drawings before you see them?
steps.today: The tester can run on the finished screens if you switch it on. It no longer tries early designs.
steps.checked: Read the live rule file today.
steps.problem: The old system ran it on every design before your first deck. It caught confusing designs early, but added waiting to every round.
steps.proposal: Pick when it runs on drawings.

options.label: Offered on each design deck, off unless you ask
pros: No waiting unless you want it.
There when a design is large or new.
cons: You must remember to ask.

options.label: Always, before you see a design
pros: Confusing designs are caught before they reach you.
cons: Every design round takes longer.

options.label: Never on drawings
pros: Simplest.
cons: You are the first to meet a confusing design.

steps.path: The checks menu, before a build
steps.headline: Should the code review be on for every build?
steps.today: The code review is suggested on only for builds touching security, your data, background work or several devices. You can switch it either way.
steps.checked: Read the live rule file today.
steps.problem: In rounds 4 and 5 you said automatic code reviews are useful and not to lose them without thought. It has the strongest record of real finds.
steps.proposal: Pick its starting position on the checks menu.

options.label: On for every build; you can switch it off
pros: Mistakes are caught without you asking.
cons: Small builds wait a few minutes more.

options.label: On only for risky builds, as today
pros: Small builds stay quick.
cons: I judge what counts as risky.

options.label: Off unless you switch it on
pros: Nothing runs unasked.
cons: Easy to forget on the build that needed it.

steps.headline: May I tell the safety scanner to ignore five made-up ids?
steps.today: 18 saved steps of this work exist only on this computer. The scanner that guards every backup refuses to send them.
steps.problem: One old step holds five practice-app ids that look like passwords to the scanner. They are not secrets, and I am not allowed to rewrite saved history.
steps.proposal: Yes adds those five exact lines to the scanner's ignore list and backs everything up. Nothing else is loosened. No leaves the work on this computer only.

steps.path: A deck link opened again after Submit
steps.headline: What should reopening an answered deck do?
steps.today: The link dies on Submit. If I serve the deck again, it opens empty and your earlier answers are filed beside it.
steps.problem: The tester read the empty deck as lost answers, and could have answered twice.
steps.proposal: Pick what a reopened deck shows.

options.label: Your answers, still editable, with a line saying when you sent them
pros: Nothing looks lost.
You can correct one answer and send again.
cons: A second Submit replaces the first; the first is kept in a dated file.

options.label: Your answers, locked
pros: A clear record.
cons: In August a locked deck read to you as "I can't click through".

options.label: Leave it: empty
pros: No change.
cons: Looks like lost answers.

steps.headline: On a phone, how should commenting on part of a picture start?
steps.today: Since this round's fixes a finger dragged across a picture draws a comment area. Before, a finger could not draw at all.
steps.problem: A swipe that starts on a picture now draws instead of scrolling the page. Not tried on a real phone.
steps.proposal: Pick how drawing starts on a touch screen. A mouse is unaffected.

options.label: Tap a "Comment on an area" button, then drag
pros: Scrolling always works.
No accidental areas.
cons: One extra tap per comment.

options.label: Leave it: any drag draws
pros: Same as with a mouse.
cons: On a page of large pictures, scrolling means aiming for the gaps.

options.label: No drawing on phones
pros: Simplest.
cons: On a phone you describe the spot in words again.

steps.headline: Should I file two idea cards from earlier rounds?
steps.today: Two ideas came up and were never filed: a simple screen sketcher inside a deck whose sketch is handed to the chat, and the app hosting deck links itself.
steps.problem: Unfiled, they exist only in these decks.
steps.proposal: Pick which to file. Filing only records the idea; nothing is built.

options.label: File both
pros: Neither is lost.
cons: Two more cards on the board.

options.label: Only the screen sketcher
pros: The one closest to your layout complaints.
cons: The hosting idea stays unrecorded.

options.label: Only app-hosted decks
pros: Would fix dead links at the root.
cons: The sketcher stays unrecorded.

options.label: Neither
pros: A shorter board.
cons: Both ideas fade.
